description: How the field is moving and where its lines are. The change questions are safe and produce forward-looking material; the ethics questions are the sharpest in the database. Never lead with the ethics half - it reads as an accusation from a stranger and as curiosity from someone who has already demonstrated they understand the work.

questions.text: What has changed in your field in the last five years that people outside have not noticed at all?
questions.lands_because: Rewards insider knowledge and produces genuinely new information for the audience. The 'not noticed' clause pushes past the obvious headline change.

questions.text: What arrived in your field with enormous noise and turned out not to matter? And what arrived quietly and changed everything?
questions.lands_because: The two-part structure produces a real assessment rather than hype or dismissal, and it works in any field with a technology or methodology cycle - which is all of them.
followups: What is being loud right now, and which category is it in?

questions.text: Is the work itself getting better or worse to do? Separate that from whether it pays better.
questions.lands_because: The instruction to separate the two is what makes it good. Autonomy, pace, surveillance, and documentation load have moved independently of compensation in most fields, and guests feel that acutely.
followups: What specifically made it worse? Or better?

questions.text: What is a rule, standard, or regulation that quietly reshaped your daily work?
questions.lands_because: Regulation is invisible from outside and enormous from inside - a building code revision, a documentation requirement, a safety standard, a disclosure rule. Asking about it signals you know work has a legal substrate.
followups: Was it a good rule badly implemented, or just a bad rule?

questions.text: What will someone entering your field in ten years never have to learn?
questions.lands_because: Forward-looking and concrete rather than speculative. It also quietly surfaces what the guest thinks is being lost, without requiring nostalgia.
followups: Does it matter that they will not know it?

questions.text: What is being lost as your field modernizes that is actually worth keeping?
questions.lands_because: Gives permission for a conservative answer without making the guest sound like a reactionary. Frequently the most heartfelt moment in a change conversation.
followups: Is anyone trying to keep it?
questions.avoid_if: The guest is a reformer or technologist whose whole position is that the old way was bad - it will read as a setup.

questions.text: Where is the gray zone in your work?
questions.lands_because: Open enough that the guest chooses the terrain, which makes it far more answerable than a specific accusation. Nearly every profession has one and can describe it if asked neutrally.
followups: How do you decide, in the moment?
Do your colleagues draw the line in the same place?

questions.text: What pressure exists in your field to cut a corner, and what does the corner actually look like?
questions.lands_because: Asks about the structure of the pressure rather than the guest's compliance with it, so it can be answered without self-incrimination. The concrete second half prevents an abstract dodge.
questions.avoid_if: The guest is personally under scrutiny for exactly this.

questions.text: Have you ever refused to do something? What happened?
questions.lands_because: Casts the guest as the person with a line rather than the person being investigated, which is why it produces real answers where a direct ethics question produces none.
Three words, and it maps the entire oversight structure of a profession - board, regulator, inspector, editor, peer review, or nobody at all. The 'nobody' answers are the interesting ones.
followups: When did that check last actually catch something?

questions.text: What is entirely legal and standard in your field that you think should not be?
questions.lands_because: Invites reform-minded criticism rather than confession, so guests answer it willingly. Frequently generates the most quotable line of an episode.
